newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tax to dominate debate if Japan holds snap poll.
newsitem.headline: Tax to dominate debate if Japan holds snap poll.

text.p: Tax talk will likely dominate the economic policy arena, shoving other vital issues to the sidelines, if Japan's ruling coalition decides to call a snap election this autumn, analysts say.

Sniping over a contentious rise in the consumption tax means deep discussion of much-needed economic and administrative reform would probably get short shrift as politicians scramble for seats in Japan's first Lower House election since a radical overhaul of the electoral system.
Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto on Friday denied media reports that his Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) was preparing for a Lower House poll in October.

No election need be held until next July, but analysts said Hashimoto could well lose his battle with LDP proponents of an early poll. "He's no longer able to sustain the argument that it would be better if they waited," said Jeff Young, an economist at Salomon Brothers Asia.

Should an early election be held, the LDP and its coalition partners -- the Social Democratic Party and the tiny Sakigake -- would have to defend a planned rise in the consumption tax to five percent from the current three percent next April.
"The LDP would be fighting on a pro-tax, pro-MOF (Ministry of Finance) policy," said Jesper Koll, chief economist at JP Morgan in Tokyo. "It remains to be seen how popular that is."

The conservative opposition Shinshinto has been preparing a bill to freeze the consumption tax increase -- approved by the cabinet in June -- to submit to an extraordinary session of parliament many had expected to be called in the autumn.
Voter antipathy to the consumption tax was a key cause of heavy LDP losses and a big win for the Social Democrats -- then in opposition -- in a 1989 Upper House election.
Younger members of Hashimoto's LDP, meanwhile, have already come out in favour of freezing the tax rise, which consumers, especially those with smaller incomes, strongly oppose.
But analysts say LDP leaders are unlikely to backpedal on the rise, which Finance Ministry officials say is vital given Japan's bulging budget deficit and rapidly aging population.
"The tax rise was approved by the cabinet, and if it were frozen it would discredit the cabinet very much," said Takashi Kiuchi, chief economist at the Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan.
An early poll would, meanwhile, make it tough for the government to craft an extra budget for this fiscal year.

Policy-makers had said they were waiting to see more economic data, including April-June gross domestic product figures due out this month, before deciding whether a stimulative supplementary budget for the year to next March was needed to keep the nation's economic recovery on track.

A modest extra budget of perhaps four trillion yen ($36.6 billion) had been expected, but would come later or not at all should autumn polls be held, Salomon's Young said, adding that passage of next year's budget could also be delayed.

Champions of electoral reform, enacted in 1994 by an anti-LDP coalition, had argued it would spur true policy debate -- a rarity in a system dominated by personality, pork barrel and political machines.
Instead of the old multi-seat electoral districts, the new system combines 300 single-seat districts with the election of 200 other members by proportional representation.

But economists are doubtful about prospects for concrete proposals that might actually be implemented, although politicians on the campaign trail are likely to pay lip service to the need for drastic reforms such as streamlining government, revising the tax system, and deregulating the economy. "The risk is that you have a very immature, populist election debate," Koll said.
